PIECE-RATE COMPENSATION AGREEMENT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Acme Corp

PIECE-RATE COMPENSATION DECLARATION
Acme Corp and Jordan Alex Lee state the following concerning Jordan Alex Lee's piece-rate compensation, effective October 1, 2026. Jordan Alex Lee's piece rate is $2.50 per unit per each garment sewn and inspected. Jordan Alex Lee's piece-rate earnings for a pay period are calculated by multiplying the number of qualifying units Jordan Alex Lee completes by the applicable piece rate. Consistent with California Labor Code § 226.2, Acme Corp compensates Jordan Alex Lee for rest and recovery periods and other nonproductive time separately from, and in addition to, Jordan Alex Lee's piece-rate compensation; that separate compensation and the piece-rate compensation described above are not combined, averaged together, or offset against one another for purposes of meeting the pay requirements that apply to each.

THE CORE REQUIREMENT: REST, RECOVERY, AND NONPRODUCTIVE TIME PAID SEPARATELY
California law governing piece-rate compensation applies to Jordan Alex Lee for any pay period in which Jordan Alex Lee is compensated on a piece-rate basis, and it does not limit or alter minimum wage or overtime requirements, or Acme Corp's obligation to compensate Jordan Alex Lee for all hours worked under any other statute or local ordinance. This law defines "applicable minimum wage" as the highest of the federal, state, or local minimum wage applicable to the employment, and defines "other nonproductive time" as time under Acme Corp's control, excluding rest and recovery periods, that is not directly related to the piece-rate activity. For any pay period in which Jordan Alex Lee is compensated on a piece-rate basis, California law requires that Jordan Alex Lee be compensated for rest and recovery periods and other nonproductive time separately from any piece-rate compensation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "This section shall apply for employees who are compensated on a piece-rate basis for any work performed during a pay period. This section shall not be construed to limit or alter minimum wage or overtime compensation requirements, or the obligation to compensate employees for all hours worked under any other statute or local ordinance. For the purposes of this section, “applicable minimum wage” means the highest of the federal, state, or local minimum wage that is applicable to the employment, and “other nonproductive time” means time under the employer’s control, exclusive of rest and recovery periods, that is not directly related to the activity being compensated on a piece-rate basis."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226.2 (preamble), Cal. Lab. Code § 226.2 (unnumbered introductory paragraph) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=226.2.)
  "(a) For employees compensated on a piece-rate basis during a pay period, the following shall apply for that pay period:(1) Employees shall be compensated for rest and recovery periods and other nonproductive time separate from any piece-rate compensation."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226.2(a)(1), Cal. Lab. Code § 226.2, subd. (a)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=226.2.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute — used as evidence of California's specific piece-rate compensation requirements, not as a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee. Piece-rate pay itself is lawful everywhere; California's requirement that rest, recovery, and other nonproductive time be compensated separately, on top of piece-rate earnings, is a distinctly California rule, and most states impose no comparable separate-compensation requirement for piece-rate workers. The statute itself defines "applicable minimum wage" and "other nonproductive time," but it does not define "rest and recovery periods" anywhere within its own text — that phrase is used, not defined, in this section; this clause does not assert that some other statute (such as the general rest-period requirement in Labor Code § 226.7 or an Industrial Welfare Commission wage order) supplies that definition, only that § 226.2 itself does not. The two quoted passages below (the definitions preamble and paragraph (a)(1)) both come from the same statutory section, § 226.2 — treated as one source, not independent corroborating sources for one another. This clause states the general separate-compensation rule only; the required minimum rate of pay for that time, the wage-statement itemization it triggers, and the now-expired transitional safe harbor for past noncompliance are addressed in separate clauses in this set.

THE MINIMUM RATE FOR REST AND RECOVERY PERIOD PAY
California law sets a floor for how Jordan Alex Lee's rest and recovery periods must be paid: Jordan Alex Lee must be compensated for rest and recovery periods at a regular hourly rate no less than the higher of (i) an average hourly rate, calculated by dividing Jordan Alex Lee's total compensation for the workweek — excluding compensation for rest and recovery periods and any overtime premium — by Jordan Alex Lee's total hours worked during the workweek, excluding rest and recovery periods; or (ii) the applicable minimum wage. For a semimonthly payroll, California law permits Acme Corp to pay Jordan Alex Lee at least the applicable minimum wage rate for rest and recovery periods together with other wages for the payroll period in which they occurred, with any additional amount owed under the average-hourly-rate calculation payable no later than the payday for the next regular payroll period.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(3) (A) Employees shall be compensated for rest and recovery periods at a regular hourly rate that is no less than the higher of:(i) An average hourly rate determined by dividing the total compensation for the workweek, exclusive of compensation for rest and recovery periods and any premium compensation for overtime, by the total hours worked during the workweek, exclusive of rest and recovery periods.(ii) The applicable minimum wage."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226.2(a)(3)(A), Cal. Lab. Code § 226.2, subd. (a)(3)(A) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=226.2.)
  "(B) For employers who pay on a semimonthly basis, employees shall be compensated at least at the applicable minimum wage rate for the rest and recovery periods together with other wages for the payroll period during which the rest and recovery periods occurred. Any additional compensation required for those employees pursuant to clause (i) of subparagraph (A) is payable no later than the payday for the next regular payroll period."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226.2(a)(3)(B), Cal. Lab. Code § 226.2, subd. (a)(3)(B) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=226.2.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute — used as evidence of California's specific piece-rate compensation requirements, not as a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee. Piece-rate pay itself is lawful everywhere; California's requirement that rest, recovery, and other nonproductive time be compensated separately, on top of piece-rate earnings, is a distinctly California rule, and most states impose no comparable separate-compensation requirement for piece-rate workers. Both quoted passages come from the same statutory paragraph, § 226.2(a)(3) — subparagraphs (A) and (B) — treated as one source, not independent corroborating sources for one another. The "higher of" comparison in subparagraph (A) is calculated per workweek even where wages are paid semimonthly; subparagraph (B) is a payroll-timing accommodation for semimonthly payers, not a different rate floor — it lets the true-up land on the following payday rather than requiring same-period computation. This clause does not calculate any particular employee's actual average hourly rate for any actual workweek; that arithmetic depends on real pay and hours data this clause does not have.

THE MINIMUM RATE FOR OTHER NONPRODUCTIVE TIME, AND HOW THE HOURS ARE COUNTED
California law requires that Jordan Alex Lee be compensated for other nonproductive time at an hourly rate no less than the applicable minimum wage. Acme Corp may determine the amount of Jordan Alex Lee's other nonproductive time either through actual records or through Acme Corp's reasonable estimates, whether for a group of employees or for Jordan Alex Lee individually. Separately, an employer who pays an hourly rate of at least the applicable minimum wage for all hours worked, in addition to any piece-rate compensation, is deemed in compliance with the other-nonproductive-time pay requirement without a separate hourly nonproductive-time calculation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(4) Employees shall be compensated for other nonproductive time at an hourly rate that is no less than the applicable minimum wage."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226.2(a)(4), Cal. Lab. Code § 226.2, subd. (a)(4) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=226.2.)
  "(5) The amount of other nonproductive time may be determined either through actual records or the employer’s reasonable estimates, whether for a group of employees or for a particular employee, of other nonproductive time worked during the pay period."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226.2(a)(5), Cal. Lab. Code § 226.2, subd. (a)(5) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=226.2.)
  "(7) An employer who, in addition to paying any piece-rate compensation, pays an hourly rate of at least the applicable minimum wage for all hours worked, shall be deemed in compliance with paragraph (4)."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226.2(a)(7), Cal. Lab. Code § 226.2, subd. (a)(7) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=226.2.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute — used as evidence of California's specific piece-rate compensation requirements, not as a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee. Piece-rate pay itself is lawful everywhere; California's requirement that rest, recovery, and other nonproductive time be compensated separately, on top of piece-rate earnings, is a distinctly California rule, and most states impose no comparable separate-compensation requirement for piece-rate workers. The three quoted passages below all come from the same statutory subdivision, § 226.2(a) — paragraphs (4), (5), and (7) — treated as one source, not independent corroborating sources for one another. This clause does not restate paragraph (6) of the same subdivision, which limits — but does not eliminate — an employer's exposure to statutory civil penalties (though not the underlying wage liability itself) for a good-faith error in estimating other-nonproductive-time hours, provided the employer met the wage-statement and payment conditions that paragraph separately specifies; that narrower point is not asserted here. This clause does not determine, for any actual employee or pay period, what qualifies as "other nonproductive time" versus time directly related to the piece-rate activity — that is a fact-specific characterization the statute leaves to be applied to particular circumstances.

THE PIECE-RATE-SPECIFIC ADDITION TO THE ITEMIZED WAGE STATEMENT
On top of the itemized-wage-statement categories California law requires of every employer, California law requires that Jordan Alex Lee's itemized wage statement, for any pay period in which Jordan Alex Lee is compensated on a piece-rate basis, separately state: the total hours of Jordan Alex Lee's compensable rest and recovery periods, the rate of compensation for that time, and the gross wages paid for those periods during the pay period; and, unless Acme Corp instead pays Jordan Alex Lee an hourly rate of at least the applicable minimum wage for all hours worked, the total hours of Jordan Alex Lee's other nonproductive time, the rate of compensation for that time, and the gross wages paid for that time during the pay period.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(2) The itemized statement required by subdivision (a) of Section 226 shall, in addition to the other items specified in that subdivision, separately state the following, to which the provisions of Section 226 shall also be applicable:(A) The total hours of compensable rest and recovery periods, the rate of compensation, and the gross wages paid for those periods during the pay period.(B) Except for employers paying compensation for other nonproductive time in accordance with paragraph (7), the total hours of other nonproductive time, as determined under paragraph (5), the rate of compensation, and the gross wages paid for that time during the pay period."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226.2(a)(2), Cal. Lab. Code § 226.2, subd. (a)(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=226.2.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute — used as evidence of California's specific piece-rate compensation requirements, not as a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee. Piece-rate pay itself is lawful everywhere; California's requirement that rest, recovery, and other nonproductive time be compensated separately, on top of piece-rate earnings, is a distinctly California rule, and most states impose no comparable separate-compensation requirement for piece-rate workers. This clause is deliberately narrow: it covers only the two piece-rate-specific categories § 226.2(a)(2) adds to an itemized wage statement — rest-and-recovery-period totals and other-nonproductive-time totals, each broken into hours, rate, and gross wages. It does not restate the nine general items every itemized wage statement must show under Labor Code § 226(a) (gross wages, total hours, deductions, and so on), which are covered in a separate clause in this document set (the "nine required itemized statement items" clause) and are not duplicated here; § 226.2(a)(2) itself states that these piece-rate additions come "in addition to the other items specified in" § 226(a)'s subdivision, and that the general remedies and enforcement provisions of § 226 also apply to these added items. This clause does not restate the separate exception in § 226.2(a)(2)(B) for employers who instead pay an hourly rate of at least the applicable minimum wage for all hours worked (covered in a separate clause in this set) beyond noting that the exception exists.

THE NOW-EXPIRED TRANSITIONAL SAFE HARBOR FOR PAST NONCOMPLIANCE
When California first enacted Labor Code § 226.2 (operative January 1, 2016 through December 31, 2020), that original version of the statute included a transitional affirmative defense: an employer had a defense to claims for recovery of wages, damages, liquidated damages, or statutory or civil penalties based solely on a failure to timely pay compensation due for rest and recovery periods and other nonproductive time for time periods before and including December 31, 2015, if the employer met a set of conditions by specific deadlines. Those conditions included making back payments to current and former employees for previously uncompensated or undercompensated rest, recovery, and other nonproductive time from July 1, 2012 through December 31, 2015, calculated either as the actual sums owed with interest, or as a flat 4% of the employee's gross piece-rate-period earnings during that window (reduced, up to a 1% cap, by amounts already separately paid for that time); filing a written election notice with the Department of Industrial Relations no later than July 1, 2016; and completing payments to each employee (or, for employees who could not be located, to the Labor Commissioner) no later than December 15, 2016. This transitional safe harbor is no longer operative: the statute that created it stated its own effective end date, and it was repealed as of January 1, 2021. The current version of § 226.2 contains no equivalent cure or affirmative-defense mechanism.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(b) Notwithstanding any other statute or regulation, the employer and any other person shall have an affirmative defense to any claim or cause of action for recovery of wages, damages, liquidated damages, statutory penalties, or civil penalties, including liquidated damages pursuant to Section 1194.2, statutory penalties pursuant to Section 203, premium pay pursuant to Section 226.7, and actual damages or liquidated damages pursuant to subdivision (e) of Section 226, based solely on the employer’s failure to timely pay the employee the compensation due for rest and recovery periods and other nonproductive time for time periods prior to and including December 31, 2015, if, by no later than December 15, 2016, an employer complies with all of the following:"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226.2(b) (2016-2020 version, as enacted), Stats. 2015, ch. 754, § 4 (AB 1513), adding former Cal. Lab. Code § 226.2, subd. (b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=201520160AB1513)
  "(1) The employer makes payments to each of its employees, except as specified in paragraph (2), for previously uncompensated or undercompensated rest and recovery periods and other nonproductive time from July 1, 2012, to December 31, 2015, inclusive, using one of the formulas specified in subparagraph (A) or (B):(A) The employer determines and pays the actual sums due together with accrued interest calculated in accordance with subdivision (c) of Section 98.1.(B) The employer pays each employee an amount equal to 4 percent of that employee’s gross earnings in pay periods in which any work was performed on a piece-rate basis from July 1, 2012, to December 31, 2015, inclusive, less amounts already paid to that employee, separate from piece-rate compensation, for rest and recovery periods and other nonproductive time during the same time,"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226.2(b)(1) (2016-2020 version, as enacted), Stats. 2015, ch. 754, § 4 (AB 1513), adding former Cal. Lab. Code § 226.2, subd. (b)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=201520160AB1513)
  "(3) By no later than July 1, 2016, the employer provides written notice to the department of the employer’s election to make payments to its current and former employees in accordance with the requirements of this subdivision and subdivision (c)."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226.2(b)(3) (2016-2020 version, as enacted), Stats. 2015, ch. 754, § 4 (AB 1513), adding former Cal. Lab. Code § 226.2, subd. (b)(3) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=201520160AB1513)
  "The employer calculates and begins making payments to employees as soon as reasonably feasible after it provides the notice referred to in paragraph (3) and completes the payments by no later than December 15, 2016, to each employee to whom the wages are due,"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226.2(b)(4) (2016-2020 version, as enacted), Stats. 2015, ch. 754, § 4 (AB 1513), adding former Cal. Lab. Code § 226.2, subd. (b)(4) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=201520160AB1513)
  "(k) This section shall remain in effect only until January 1, 2021, and as of that date is repealed."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226.2(k) (2016-2020 version, as enacted), Stats. 2015, ch. 754, § 4 (AB 1513), adding former Cal. Lab. Code § 226.2, subd. (k) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=201520160AB1513)

This clause is presented for historical and informational context only — it describes a mechanism that no longer exists in current law, not a currently available option. All five quoted passages below come from the same enactment: the original (2016-2020) version of § 226.2, added by Section 4 of 2015 Cal. Stats., ch. 754 (Assembly Bill 1513) — treated as one source, not independent corroborating sources for one another. This clause summarizes only the payment-formula and deadline mechanics; it does not restate every condition and exclusion the original statute attached to the defense (for example, the separate accurate-statement requirement accompanying each payment, the narrower good-faith-error cure window, the tolling of the statute of limitations during the election period, or the several categories of pre-existing claims the statute carved out of the defense's reach entirely), and it takes no position on whether any particular employer actually made a timely, compliant election and payment during the window that existed. Because the deadlines this mechanism depended on (July 1, 2016 and December 15, 2016) and the mechanism's own repeal date (January 1, 2021) have all passed, this clause is included to explain why the safe harbor is no longer available, not to describe a present cure path for current noncompliance.

WHAT "PIECE-RATE COMPENSATION" MEANS: NO DEDICATED STATUTORY DEFINITION
California's piece-rate compensation statute does not itself define the term "piece-rate compensation" or "piece-rate basis"; the statute defines only "applicable minimum wage" and "other nonproductive time," and otherwise uses the phrase "compensated on a piece-rate basis" without further elaboration. The closest general statutory anchor is California's broad definition of "wages," which lists "piece" as one of several methods by which the amount of labor compensation may be fixed or ascertained, alongside time, task, and commission basis. Beyond that general listing, California statute leaves "piece-rate compensation" to its ordinary usage: compensation calculated by reference to a completed unit of production, or a fixed amount per task, rather than by the hour.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "For the purposes of this section, “applicable minimum wage” means the highest of the federal, state, or local minimum wage that is applicable to the employment, and “other nonproductive time” means time under the employer’s control, exclusive of rest and recovery periods, that is not directly related to the activity being compensated on a piece-rate basis."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 226.2 (defined terms), Cal. Lab. Code § 226.2 (unnumbered introductory paragraph) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=226.2.)
  "“Wages” includes all amounts for labor performed by employees of every description, whether the amount is fixed or ascertained by the standard of time, task, piece, commission basis, or other method of calculation."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 200(a), Cal. Lab. Code § 200, subd. (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=200.)

Piece-rate pay itself is lawful everywhere; California's requirement that rest, recovery, and other nonproductive time be compensated separately, on top of piece-rate earnings, is a distinctly California rule, and most states impose no comparable separate-compensation requirement for piece-rate workers. This clause reports an absence, not a finding: no statutory definition of "piece-rate compensation" or "piece-rate basis" was located within § 226.2 or within the general wage definitions in § 200 of the same code; this clause does not assert that no such definition exists anywhere in California law, regulation, or agency guidance (for example, in Division of Labor Standards Enforcement guidance or Industrial Welfare Commission wage orders), only that this clause's own search of these two primary statutory sources did not find one. The two quoted passages below come from two different statutory sections (§ 226.2 and § 200) and are independent of each other in that sense, though both are used only to show what the statutory text does and does not define, not to establish any operative rule beyond that.

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Jordan Alex Lee acknowledges having received and reviewed this Piece-Rate Compensation Agreement — Information Sheet, and understands that it describes Acme Corp's piece-rate pay structure and the separate compensation Jordan Alex Lee receives for rest and recovery periods and other nonproductive time. Jordan Alex Lee may direct any question about a specific wage statement or pay calculation to Acme Corp.

Jordan Alex Lee (Employee): _______________  Date: October 1, 2026

Jordan Alex Lee, on behalf of Acme Corp: _______________  Date: October 1, 2026

Signed at: San Francisco, California

expectedJSON.body: When California first enacted Labor Code § 226.2 (operative January 1, 2016 through December 31, 2020), that original version of the statute included a transitional affirmative defense: an employer had a defense to claims for recovery of wages, damages, liquidated damages, or statutory or civil penalties based solely on a failure to timely pay compensation due for rest and recovery periods and other nonproductive time for time periods before and including December 31, 2015, if the employer met a set of conditions by specific deadlines. Those conditions included making back payments to current and former employees for previously uncompensated or undercompensated rest, recovery, and other nonproductive time from July 1, 2012 through December 31, 2015, calculated either as the actual sums owed with interest, or as a flat 4% of the employee's gross piece-rate-period earnings during that window (reduced, up to a 1% cap, by amounts already separately paid for that time); filing a written election notice with the Department of Industrial Relations no later than July 1, 2016; and completing payments to each employee (or, for employees who could not be located, to the Labor Commissioner) no later than December 15, 2016. This transitional safe harbor is no longer operative: the statute that created it stated its own effective end date, and it was repealed as of January 1, 2021. The current version of § 226.2 contains no equivalent cure or affirmative-defense mechanism.

expectedJSON.body: California's piece-rate compensation statute does not itself define the term "piece-rate compensation" or "piece-rate basis"; the statute defines only "applicable minimum wage" and "other nonproductive time," and otherwise uses the phrase "compensated on a piece-rate basis" without further elaboration. The closest general statutory anchor is California's broad definition of "wages," which lists "piece" as one of several methods by which the amount of labor compensation may be fixed or ascertained, alongside time, task, and commission basis. Beyond that general listing, California statute leaves "piece-rate compensation" to its ordinary usage: compensation calculated by reference to a completed unit of production, or a fixed amount per task, rather than by the hour.

citations.quote: For the purposes of this section, “applicable minimum wage” means the highest of the federal, state, or local minimum wage that is applicable to the employment, and “other nonproductive time” means time under the employer’s control, exclusive of rest and recovery periods, that is not directly related to the activity being compensated on a piece-rate basis.

“Wages” includes all amounts for labor performed by employees of every description, whether the amount is fixed or ascertained by the standard of time, task, piece, commission basis, or other method of calculation.
